Memory Match move-count vs timed memory games

A current comparison of Memory Match’s two-card move counter with timed formats, including the seeded board and lack of saved V2 records.

By NoCharge Editorial·Reviewed by NoCharge Editorial·Published August 27, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Check the current platform.

Use the public pages behind this explanation.

Open the ArcadeReview PrivacyKeyboard-only play notes

Bottom line: NoCharge Memory Match has no countdown. It displays the number of two-card attempts on the current board; it does not save a best score or rank players.

Compare the mechanics, not every game

AspectNoCharge Memory MatchA timed memory format may use
Board4×4, eight symbol pairsVaries by game
MeasureOne move per two-card attemptElapsed time or a countdown
PressureNo clock or speed bonusDepends on that game’s rules
RecordCurrent board’s move count only; reset clears itDepends on that game’s storage model

What “good” means here

Eight moves is the theoretical minimum for eight pairs if every location is known before the first choice. In ordinary play, the first attempts reveal information. A mismatch still counts as a move, but it can be useful if you remember both symbols and positions.

The current board is initialized from a fixed seed, so reset returns the same arrangement rather than a newly randomized layout. Repeated attempts can be used to practice a scan, but no V2 best-move record is saved automatically.

What the comparison does not claim

A move counter is not a measure of intelligence or a promise of memory improvement. Timed alternatives also differ from one another; check their own rules instead of assuming every timed game uses the same design.

Try a deliberate top-to-bottom scan and use the live counter as a description of this run. The current game page explains the controls and reset behavior.
